title: The hierarchical lattice
subtitle: An ultrametric group whose blocks fall into L^d congruent children.
summary: The hierarchical lattice is the direct sum of countably many copies of (Z/LZ)^d, with an ultrametric whose balls have exactly L^(dn) points. Each ball splits into L^d congruent children, every pair of vertices in different children of a ball sits at the top distance of that ball, and power kernels are summable exactly when their exponent exceeds the dimension. These three facts are what make block decimation close on one-variable laws.
text:
The hierarchical lattice $\mathbb H^d_L$ is the abelian group of finite sequences with entries in $(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^d$, carrying the ultrametric in which two vertices are at distance $L^k$ when the last coordinate at which they differ is the $k$-th. Its balls are nested subgroups, of exactly $L^{dn}$ vertices at radius $L^n$, and each ball splits into $L^d$ congruent children. Every pair of vertices in different children of a ball lies at the top distance of that ball, so a coupling that charges each pair according to its distance charges all pairs between two children at one rate, which depends only on the two block sums. This is the structure that makes block decimation an exact operation on a single variable, and it is why the model appears throughout the rigorous theory of the renormalisation group [@bauerschmidt-brydges-slade-2019]. The lattice was introduced by Dyson (1969) as a one-dimensional model with long-range couplings in which a phase transition can be proved [@dyson-1969], and the group-theoretic description used here, with balls as cosets of nested subgroups, is the form in which the renormalisation group is usually set up [@bleher-sinai-1973]. A power kernel $\lVert xVert^{-d-\alpha}$ is summable exactly when $\alpha>0$, so the model with such a kernel is a long-range spin system with a finite interaction range in the only sense that matters: the total intensity at each vertex is finite. Two conventions are worth fixing at the outset. The dimension enters the lattice only through the block volume $m=L^d$ and the decay ratio $\lambda=L^{d+\alpha}=mL^{\alpha}$; any integer $m\geq2$ and any ratio $\lambda>m$ arise from some pair $(d,\alpha)$ once a scale $L$ is chosen. And the lattice is a group, so distances are translation invariant and every vertex looks like the origin. title: Hierarchical spin systems and decimation
subtitle: The block spin of a hierarchical model is distributed as a functional of independent copies of the block spin one scale down.
summary: A spin system on the hierarchical lattice with couplings constant on levels has a Hamiltonian that splits into the Hamiltonians of its children plus one interaction between their sums. Consequently the partition function and the law of a block spin are recovered from the law one scale down by an explicit operation, the free energy has an exact recursion, and the whole renormalisation group is a recursion on one-variable laws.
text: A hierarchical spin system is a spin model on $\mathbb H^d_L$ whose coupling between two vertices is a function of their level alone, so that the coupling at level $k$ has one value $J_k=JL^{-(d+\alpha)k}$. Its energy on a block splits exactly into the energies of the children of that block plus a single interaction between the child sums: pairs inside a child are at levels below the top, pairs in different children are all at the top level, and no pair inside the block is at a level above it. The partition function therefore factorises, and the law of a block spin is the image of the law one scale down under an explicit operation — block decimation — which acts on the single variable $\sum_{x\in\text{child}}\sigma_x$. This article states that identity, its iterates, and the free energy recursion that follows; the operation itself is studied in the next article and solved exactly in the Gaussian case . The identity is what is special about the lattice: on $\mathbb Z^d$ a decimation step produces an interaction that depends on the shape of the boundary between blocks, whereas here it produces one number per block. The structure is Dyson's (1969), who introduced the hierarchical approximation to prove a phase transition for power-law couplings [@dyson-1969], and it is the setting of the renormalisation analysis of Bleher and Sinai [@bleher-sinai-1973]. Only free boundary conditions are used, so every object below is finite-dimensional and every identity is exact at finite volume. title: Ultrametric block systems and the p-adic models
subtitle: What the recursion actually needs, and how little of it is specific to the hierarchical lattice.
summary: The decimation recursion uses only a nested system of blocks with a constant number of children per block. Any ultrametric group with such a system carries the same model, the same map and the same exponents: the p-adic integers with their balls, the hierarchical lattice with its subgroups, and their variants. The child decomposition and the decimation identity are proved here in that generality, and the one place where the compact and discrete cases differ is isolated.
text:
Every proof in this wiki about decimation uses exactly two facts: that the blocks of a fixed level are the cosets of a subgroup, and that each block has the same number $m$ of children. Nothing else about the hierarchical lattice is used: not the direct-sum construction, not countability, not the arithmetic of $(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^d$. This article states the construction for an arbitrary abelian group with a nested block system and proves the two structural results in that generality; the decimation identity , the map and the exponent dictionary then apply verbatim. The standard compact example is the ring of p-adic integers $\mathbb Z_p$ with the balls of the p-adic metric, which are the cosets of $p^n\mathbb Z_p$: each ball has exactly $p$ children, at every scale, forever. The models on $\mathbb Z_p$ are used in the renormalisation-group approach to conformal field theory, where the exactness of the block structure is worth the loss of translation invariance in the Euclidean sense [@abdesselam-2018]. The one point at which the two settings differ is the meaning of the volume of a block: a coset of $\Lambda_n$ in the hierarchical lattice is a finite set and its volume is its cardinality, while a ball in $\mathbb Z_p$ is uncountable and its volume is its Haar measure. The recursion sees only the ratio of the volumes of a block and its child, which is $m$ in both cases, so the two models have the same renormalisation group. Vertices at level $n$ are those in $G_n\setminus G_{n-1}$, and the shell at level $n$ is $G_n\setminus G_{n-1}$. Two examples carry the subject. For the hierarchical lattice $\mathbb H^d_L$ one takes $G_n=\Lambda_n$, the sequences supported on the first $n$ coordinates, and $m=L^d$; the blocks are finite and the volumes are cardinalities $m^n$. title: The renormalisation group map
subtitle: Decimation as an operator on one-variable laws, and the scaling that makes it autonomous.
summary: Block decimation sends the law of a child's block spin to the law of the parent's: a nonlinear operator on probability measures on the line, a Gibbs tilt of a product measure followed by summation. Rescaling the spin by L to the power minus (d+alpha)/2 makes the operators at different scales into powers of a single map, whose fixed points and linearisations carry the critical behaviour.
text: Block decimation turns the exact recursion of a hierarchical spin system into an operator $\mathcal T_b$ on probability measures on the line: take $m$ independent copies of a law, tilt them by $\exp(b\sum_{a<a'}s_as_{a'})$, and record the law of their sum. The model applies $\mathcal T_{\beta J_n}$ with $J_n$ decaying geometrically, so the sequence of operators is not autonomous; rescaling the spin by $L^{-\theta}$ with $\theta=\tfrac12(d+\alpha)$ multiplies the coupling by $L^{2\theta}$ at each step and makes the composition a power of one map $\mathcal R_\theta$. That map is the object whose fixed points, and whose linearisation at them, carry the critical behaviour: a fixed point is a self-similar block-spin law, and the eigenvalues of the derivative there are the exponents, in the way made precise in the article on exponents . Two of its properties are used constantly and are proved here: it commutes with dilations, in the sense that $\mathcal T_b$ applied to a dilated law is the dilation of $\mathcal T_{b\lambda^2}$ applied to the law, and it is continuous on laws supported in a fixed compact set. The construction is that of Bleher and Sinai (1973), who studied the transformation directly for Dyson's model [@bleher-sinai-1973], and it is the map developed from scratch in the renormalisation-group treatment of lattice field theory [@bauerschmidt-brydges-slade-2019]. Nothing in this article depends on the model being Gaussian or Ising; the two cases are worked out in the Gaussian article and, in its own form, in the percolation article . title: The Gaussian renormalisation group
subtitle: On Gaussian laws the decimation closes on the variance, and the critical fixed point has multiplier L to the alpha.
summary: For a Gaussian prior, the law of a block spin stays Gaussian and its variance obeys a fractional linear recursion that is solved in closed form. The critical intensity is the reciprocal of the total kernel mass, the susceptibility is exactly beta_c over beta_c minus beta, and the recursion, written in the dimensionless coupling, has a nonzero fixed point with multiplier L to the alpha; hence the correlation-length exponent is one over alpha and the two-point exponent is two minus alpha.
text: With a Gaussian single-spin prior the decimation operator preserves Gaussianity: the tilt is quadratic and the sum is linear, so the block spin of a Gaussian model is Gaussian and the whole orbit is described by one number, its variance. The recursion for that variance is fractional linear, so it is solved in closed form: the block-spin variance at scale $n$ is $L^{dn}$ divided by $1-\beta\sum_{x\ne0}J(\lVert x\rVert)$ truncated to the first $n$ shells. Three consequences follow without further work. The critical intensity is the reciprocal of the total kernel mass, so the interaction is summable exactly in the regime in which the intensity is finite; the susceptibility is exactly $(\beta_c-\beta)^{-1}\beta_c$; and the recursion written in the dimensionless variable $u_n=\beta J_nv_n$ has a nonzero fixed point whose multiplier is $L^\alpha$. The multiplier is the point of the exercise. In the dictionary of the exponent article , a multiplier $\lambda_1=L^\alpha$ at the critical fixed point gives $\nu=\log L/\log\lambda_1=1/\alpha$, which is the classical long-range value; together with the block-spin growth exponent $\theta=\tfrac12(d+\alpha)$, which the normalisation of the recursion at the autonomous scale forces, it gives $\kappa=\alpha$ and hence $\eta=2-\alpha$. These are the values tabulated for long-range interactions by Fisher, Ma and Nickel [@fisher-ma-nickel-1972], and they are exact for this model. The Gaussian model is the one case of the hierarchical recursion that is solved in closed form, and it is the reference point for the others: the non-Gaussian fixed point of Bleher and Sinai merges with it at $\alpha=d/2$ and governs the critical behaviour above that value, and the percolation exponents of the percolation article coincide with the Gaussian ones in the sense that its two-point exponent is also $2-\alpha$. subtitle: Why the quartic coupling is relevant above half the dimension, and what it is a computation of.
summary: At the Gaussian fixed point the linearised decimation map is triangular in the basis of even monomials, and its diagonal entries are L^(d(1-k)+k alpha) for the monomial of degree 2k. The first entry is the variance multiplier; the second is the eigenvalue of the quartic coupling, which exceeds one exactly when alpha exceeds half the dimension. The relevance of the quartic term, the crossover at alpha = d/2 and the upper critical dimension four of the nearest-neighbour model are therefore one computation.
text: The Gaussian renormalisation group computes one eigenvalue: the variance of the block spin is multiplied by $L^{\alpha}$ per scale at the critical point, and that gives $\nu=1/\alpha$. That is the first of a family. At the Gaussian fixed point the linearised map is triangular in the basis of even monomials, and the monomial $s^{2k}$ carries the eigenvalue $$\lambda_{2k}=L^{\,d(1-k)+k\alpha},$$ of which the variance direction is $k=1$. The next one, $\lambda_4=L^{2\alpha-d}$, is the eigenvalue of the quartic coupling, and it exceeds one exactly when $\alpha>d/2$. So the statement that the quartic coupling is irrelevant below half the dimension, which the truncations article and the fixed-point article both rely on, is not an extra input: it is the second diagonal entry of the same matrix. The formula also reproduces the familiar thresholds. A nearest-neighbour model has $\alpha=2$ in this language, and then $\lambda_4=L^{4-d}$: marginal at $d=4$, relevant below it, irrelevant above. That is the upper critical dimension, and the crossover at $\alpha=d/2$ is the same equation $\lambda_4=1$ read in the other variable. The classical long-range exponent values and the threshold are those of Fisher, Ma and Nickel [@fisher-ma-nickel-1972]; what this article adds is that in the hierarchical model they follow from the linearisation by a computation short enough to give in full. Two limits on the statement are worth naming at the outset. It is a statement about the Gaussian fixed point, so it says when that fixed point is unstable, not what replaces it; the replacement is the subject of the Bleher-Sinai article . And it is a statement about finite-dimensional truncations of the space of perturbations, triangular in the monomial basis; the eigenvalues of the full map on a Banach space of interactions require the analytic estimates of the rigorous analyses. title: Critical exponents from the renormalisation group
subtitle: Two numbers from the fixed point, and the algebra that turns them into the exponents.
summary: The exponents of a hierarchical model are read off from its fixed point: one from the multiplier of the linearised map, giving the correlation-length exponent, and one from the growth of the block spin, giving the susceptibility exponent and hence the two-point exponent. The scaling relations are then algebra, and hyperscaling is the one hypothesis that is not automatic.

title: Corrections to scaling
subtitle: The second eigenvalue, and why a power law is only ever the first term.
summary: Near a fixed point the orbit approaches along the stable directions, so every power law carries corrections from the second eigenvalue. In the hierarchical model the corrections are geometric in the scale and therefore pure powers of the correlation length, one for each subleading eigenvalue, with exponent omega equal to minus the logarithm of the subleading eigenvalue over the logarithm of the scale; a complex pair makes them oscillate in the logarithm of the length, and an eigenvalue tending to one makes them logarithmic.
text:
A critical exponent describes the leading term of an asymptotic expansion, and the expansion has further terms. In the hierarchical model those terms are especially simple: a perturbation of the fixed point in a direction whose eigenvalue is $\lambda$ is multiplied by $\lambda$ per scale, and since the scale of the critical theory is the correlation length, the perturbation appears as a power of $\xi$, with exponent $-\log\lvert\lambdavert/\log L$. The leading irrelevant direction therefore gives a relative correction of order $\xi^{-\omega}$ with $\omega=-\log\lvert\lambda_2vert/\log L$, and each further eigenvalue gives one more power. Three features are worth stating before the derivation. The corrections are geometric in the scale , so in the hierarchical model they are pure powers rather than powers times logarithms; the same is true in the Euclidean theory only after resummation. A complex conjugate pair of eigenvalues replaces the power by a power times a cosine of the logarithm of the length, which is the oscillatory correction that the numerical literature reports for the hierarchical model [@gawedzki-kupiainen-1983]. And when the second eigenvalue tends to one, as it does at the marginal exponent, the correction exponent tends to zero and the corrections become logarithmic, which is why the marginal case needs its own analysis. Nothing here is specific to the model: the argument is the spectral expansion of the orbit, and the model determines the eigenvalues. What the hierarchical model contributes is that the expansion is in the scale with no mixing between scales, so the correction structure can be written down exactly given the spectrum. title: The Bleher–Sinai fixed point
subtitle: Above the threshold a non-Gaussian law is self-similar, and its multiplier is not one over alpha.
summary: For kernel exponent above half the dimension the critical orbit of the hierarchical recursion converges to a self-similar law that is not Gaussian: the fixed point of Bleher and Sinai and of Gawedzki and Kupiainen. Its linearisation has a simple leading eigenvalue, which gives a correlation-length exponent different from the classical one over alpha, and a spectrum whose next eigenvalue controls corrections to scaling, sometimes oscillating.
text:
For $\alpha$ above half the dimension the critical orbit of the hierarchical recursion does not settle at a Gaussian law. It converges instead to a self-similar law $
u^*$ which is symmetric, has exponential tails and finite variance, and is not Gaussian; the multiplier of the linearised map there is a number $\lambda_1>1$ other than $L^{\alpha}$, and the correlation-length exponent $
u=\log L/\log\lambda_1$ therefore differs from the classical value $1/\alpha$. The existence of such a law, the convergence of the orbit to it, and the reading of the indices from the linearisation are the results of Bleher and Sinai (1973, 1975) for Dyson's model [@bleher-sinai-1973] [@bleher-sinai-1975]; the local analysis of the map around the fixed point, including the $\varepsilon$-expansion and the normal form of the unstable manifold, is due to Gawedzki and Kupiainen [@gawedzki-kupiainen-1983]. The threshold $\alpha=d/2$ is where the classical long-range exponents stop being the Ising ones; it is the value at which the quartic coupling becomes relevant at the Gaussian fixed point, as computed in the spectrum article . At $\alpha=d/2$ the classical values are $
u=2/d$, $\eta=2-d/2$, $\delta=3$ and $ eta_{\mathrm{o}}=	frac12$, which are the mean-field values with $

The fixed point is not explicit: it is the solution of a nonlinear integral equation, and its existence is proved by a combination of an invariant cone, a truncation and a contraction. And the map is not contracting everywhere: the leading eigenvalue exceeds one, so the interesting statement is about the unstable manifold of dimension two, which is what makes the critical exponents well defined at all. title: Koch and Wittwer's non-Gaussian fixed point
subtitle: Convergent expansions for a fixed point with unbounded spins, large fields included.
summary: Koch and Wittwer proved the existence of a non-Gaussian fixed point of the hierarchical renormalisation map, in the hierarchical approximation of the three-dimensional phi-fourth fixed point, by a method that treats the large-field region: Borel summation brings the region where the perturbative expansion fails back into it, so that the theory is described by convergent expansions. The companion papers study the transformation itself, with its beta function and the relation between Dyson's and Gallavotti's hierarchies, and treat the Dyson-Baker hierarchy.
text: A fixed point of the hierarchical renormalisation map that is not quadratic is the critical theory of the scalar model above the marginal exponent, and the two general routes to it leave a gap. The theorem of Bleher and Sinai proves existence in a class of measures, but its statement is qualitative and its hypotheses are those of a parameter range; the epsilon expansion of Gawedzki and Kupiainen describes a neighbourhood of the marginal exponent. Koch and Wittwer closed the gap for the hierarchical model with unbounded spins by proving that the non-Gaussian fixed point governing the infrared behaviour of the three-dimensional critical theory exists, and that the theory around it is described by convergent expansions [@koch-wittwer-1986]. The obstacle they had to remove is the large-field problem . With a phi-fourth single-spin distribution the spins are unbounded, and the region in which the field is large carries most of the measure while lying outside the reach of the perturbative expansion; a renormalisation-group argument that controls the small-field region alone does not define the map. Their method handles that region by Borel summation, which resums the perturbation series so that the large-field region is incorporated into the perturbative one, and improves on the analyticity techniques of Gawedzki and Kupiainen's hierarchy-model papers [@gawedzki-kupiainen-1982] [@gawedzki-kupiainen-tirozzi-1984]. The result is a fixed point with a convergent expansion around it, at a specific parameter value and without a small parameter. The two companion papers complete the picture. The paper of 1991 studies the renormalisation transformation for scalar hierarchical models as an object in its own right: the beta function written for the transformation, its asymptotic behaviour, and the connection between the hierarchical models of Dyson and of Gallavotti [@koch-wittwer-1991]. The paper of 1994 proves a nontrivial fixed point for the Dyson-Baker hierarchical model, the variant whose blocks come from an expanding map of the interval [@koch-wittwer-1994]. The quadratic fixed point exists for exactly one curvature at each coupling, is computed in the Gaussian article , and is the fixed point that loses stability at the marginal exponent; the non-quadratic fixed point is the one that takes over. Because the single-spin distribution has unbounded support, the domain of the map is not a space of bounded functions: the tilt and the constraint allow configurations in which one child carries an arbitrarily large spin, and the integral defining $\mathcal V_bV$ is finite only because the prior decays. title: Abdesselam's trajectory between two fixed points
subtitle: A whole orbit of the renormalisation group, from the Gaussian fixed point to the nontrivial one.
summary: A fixed point describes one scale-invariant theory; a trajectory between two fixed points describes the whole crossover from the ultraviolet to the infrared. Abdesselam constructed such a trajectory rigorously and nonperturbatively for a three-dimensional phi-fourth model with modified propagator, joining the Gaussian fixed point to an analogue of the Wilson-Fisher fixed point, by a fixed point argument in a Banach space of sequences which perturbs a nonlinear one-dimensional iteration.
text: The renormalisation group of a lattice field theory is a map on a space of interactions, one step per scale, and most rigorous results about it are local: a fixed point, its stable and unstable manifolds, and the behaviour of orbits near it. A complete trajectory is a global object instead, an orbit defined at every scale and asymptotic at one end to the ultraviolet Gaussian fixed point and at the other to the nontrivial infrared one. Abdesselam constructed such a trajectory rigorously and nonperturbatively for the three-dimensional $\varphi^4$ model with a modified free propagator [@abdesselam-2007], joining the Gaussian fixed point to an analogue of the Wilson-Fisher fixed point of the kind constructed by Brydges, Mitter and Scoppola [@brydges-mitter-scoppola-2003]. Two features of the construction matter for this wiki. It does not use the hierarchical approximation — the map is the Euclidean one — and yet the unperturbed problem it perturbs is a nonlinear one-dimensional iteration of exactly the kind the hierarchical model provides, with the perturbation supplied by the modified propagator [@abdesselam-2009]. The hierarchical recursion is therefore not an analogy for the Euclidean renormalisation group in this work but its first approximation, and the trajectory is recovered from the one-dimensional flow by a fixed-point argument in a space of sequences of effective potentials. The modification of the propagator is what makes the argument close: it suppresses the fluctuations at each scale by a fixed amount, so that the Euclidean step is a bounded perturbation of the hierarchical one. Whether the trajectory can be transported to the unmodified propagator is a separate question, and the construction is a statement about the modified model. Definitions and setting # The renormalisation group is the following operation, in the form used in the renormalisation-group treatment of lattice fields [@bauerschmidt-brydges-slade-2019]. One fixes a fluctuation covariance $C$, a positive definite kernel on the lattice, and a decomposition of it into pieces $C=\sum_jC_j$ indexed by scale. Given an effective potential $V_j$ at scale $j$, one defines $$e^{-V_{j+1}(\varphi)}=\int e^{-V_j(\varphi+\zeta)}\,\mu_{C_j}(d\zeta),$$ the convolution of the Boltzmann weight with the Gaussian measure of covariance $C_j$, followed by the rescalings of field and position that put the result in a fixed normal form. The map $V_j\mapsto V_{j+1}$ is the renormalisation step, and a fixed point of the step is a scale-invariant theory. A trajectory between two fixed points is a sequence $(V_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$ of effective potentials, each in the domain of the map, such that $V_{j+1}$ is the image of $V_j$ for every $j$, and such that $V_j$ converges to the Gaussian fixed point as $j\to-\infty$ and to the nontrivial fixed point as $j\to+\infty$. The first limit is the ultraviolet, the second the infrared; the intermediate potentials describe the crossover, which is the region in which neither fixed point's linearisation controls the flow. For the hierarchical model the corresponding object is a sequence of laws $\nu_j=\mathcal R_{\theta_0,b}^{\,j}\nu_0$ under the single map of the autonomous form , and a trajectory between fixed points is an orbit whose two ends are the Gaussian and nontrivial fixed points of that map. In that case the trajectory is a property of a one-dimensional iteration and can be analysed by the methods of the fixed-point article . Then there is a sequence of effective potentials $(V_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$ satisfying the renormalisation recursion exactly, asymptotic to the ultraviolet Gaussian fixed point as $j\to-\infty$ and to the nontrivial infrared fixed point as $j\to+\infty$. title: Renormalisation for hierarchical percolation
subtitle: Cluster amplification is the relevant direction, and the triangle threshold is three alpha against d.
summary: For long-range percolation on the hierarchical lattice the renormalisation group acts on clusters rather than on a one-variable law, and its relevant direction is the amplification of large clusters across a block. The critical two-point function decays like the distance to the power minus d minus alpha for every exponent in the long-range range, and the triangle diagram converges exactly when three alpha is below d, which is where the model stops being mean-field.
text: Long-range percolation on the hierarchical lattice has bond intensities $J\lVert x-y\rVert^{-d-\alpha}$, so the intensity of the edge between two vertices depends only on their level, and the model inherits the child decomposition of the lattice. Its renormalisation group does not act on the law of one number: the state of a block is the partition of its vertices into clusters, and the operation of decimation is the passage from the cluster partition of the children to that of the block. What survives from the spin case is the amplification: two large clusters in sibling blocks are joined with probability comparable to $\beta J_n$ times their product of sizes, so a block whose clusters are atypically large produces a parent whose clusters are larger still. That mechanism gives the exact exponents. At criticality the expected size of the restricted cluster of the origin in $\Lambda_n$ grows like $L^{\alpha n}$ — the growth exponent $\kappa=\alpha$ of the exponent dictionary — and the critical connection probability between vertices at distance $L^n$ is of order $L^{-(d-\alpha)n}$, so $\eta=2-\alpha$ for every $0<\alpha<d$. This is unambiguous in the mean-field region, where the second moment of the cluster size diverges, and it holds beyond it as well; the theorem is Hutchcroft's, and it is the only case in which the two-point exponent is known across the whole long-range range [@hutchcroft-hierarchical-2021]. The phase transition itself is classical: $\beta_c$ is finite exactly when $\alpha<d$, and there is no infinite cluster at $\beta_c$ [@koval-meester-trapman-2012]. The renormalisation group enters at the level of exponents, and the question it answers is why the model is mean-field below $\alpha=d/3$ and not above: the triangle diagram is a convergent sum below that value and a divergent one above it, and the diagram is computable here because the lattice is ultrametric. title: Hierarchical models with continuous symmetry
subtitle: With a vector spin the block direction does not settle at criticality, and the marginal exponent is decided by a slowly varying factor.
summary: For the r-component hierarchical model the decimation map acts on laws on R^r by the same tilt, and it commutes with rotations. Bleher and Major proved Dyson's conjecture for this model: at the marginal kernel exponent a transition exists exactly when the level couplings are not summable, the spontaneous magnetisation vanishes at the critical temperature, and the normalised average spin still converges to the uniform law on the sphere. The Gaussian fixed point is r-independent; the continuous symmetry enters through a marginal angular direction.
text:
The $r$-component hierarchical model is the model of the decimation article with a vector spin: $\sigma_x\in\mathbb R^r$ and energy $-\sum_{\{x,y\}}J(\lVert x-yVert)\langle\sigma_x,\sigma_yangle$, with $J(L^n)=l_nL^{-(d+\alpha)n}$. Rotation invariance replaces the spin-flip symmetry, the block spin becomes a vector, and the decimation identity survives with inner products in place of products; what does not survive is the scalar picture of criticality. At the critical temperature the direction of the block spin does not concentrate: Bleher and Major proved that the normalised average spin converges in law to the uniform distribution on the sphere, while the spontaneous magnetisation vanishes [@bleher-major-2021]. The same work settles Dyson's conjecture for this model at the marginal exponent. When $\alpha=d$ the interaction is summable or not according to the level sequence: $\sum_nJ_nL^{dn}=\sum_nl_n$. Bleher and Major prove that a phase transition exists exactly when $\sum_nl_n=\infty$, so the marginal case is decided by the slowly varying factor and not by any exponent, and they prove that the transition is continuous — there is no Thouless effect, in which the magnetisation would jump. What replaces the jump is the failure of concentration of the direction at criticality: the order parameter is zero, and yet the block spin is not small. Two structural facts organise the comparison with the scalar case. The decimation map commutes with rotations, so the state of the recursion is a rotation-covariant law on $\mathbb R^r$; and the Gaussian fixed point is $r$-independent, since the tilt couples the components separately and the variance recursion is the scalar one. The exponents $\kappa=\alpha$ and $\eta=2-\alpha$ are therefore unchanged by $r$, and the $r$-dependence enters through a marginal angular direction, the hierarchical counterpart of a Goldstone mode, which is what the nontrivial fixed point acquires when the symmetry is continuous. The prior is a rotation invariant probability measure $\varrho$ on $\mathbb R^r$ with finite second moment; the two cases below are the classical spin $\varrho$ uniform on $\mathbb S^{r-1}$, and the Gaussian $\varrho=N(0,I_r)$. For $r=1$ this is the scalar model, and the inner product is the product. The block spin of $S$ is $S_S=\sum_{x\in S}\sigma_x\in\mathbb R^r$ and $\mu_n$ is its law under the Gibbs measure of $\Lambda_n$ with free boundary. title: The phi-fourth hierarchical model and its truncations
subtitle: The recursion is an integral operator on potentials; the Gaussian truncation is exact and every other truncation leaks.
summary: Written on potentials rather than on laws, the decimation step is an explicit integral operator: the effective potential of a block is minus the logarithm of a constrained convolution of the child potential. Quadratic potentials are mapped to quadratic potentials and the flow on them is the fractional linear recursion for the variance; quartic and higher truncations are not invariant, because the constrained average of a quartic generates powers of every even order. The two rigorous treatments of the resulting infinite-dimensional flow are Koch and Wittwer's fixed point and, in the Euclidean setting, the trajectory of Abdesselam.
text: In the hierarchical model with a spin prior of the form $e^{-V(s)}ds$ the state of the recursion is a potential, not a number: after one decimation step the block spin has a density whose negative logarithm is the effective potential , computed from the child potential by a constrained convolution. The recursion is exact and it is an operation on an infinite-dimensional space; the question is which finite-dimensional families it leaves invariant, and the answer is that only the quadratic one does. Write $V(s)=\tfrac{\mu}{2}s^2+\lambda s^4$; the Gaussian part flows by a fractional linear recursion solved in the Gaussian article , and the quartic part generates powers of every even order, so a two-coupling truncation is an approximation whose error is not controlled by the recursion itself [@bleher-sinai-1973]. The two rigorous treatments of the full flow are Koch and Wittwer's proof of a nontrivial fixed point for scalar hierarchical models [@koch-wittwer-1986], described in this wiki's article on it , and, in the Euclidean setting, Abdesselam's construction of a complete trajectory between the Gaussian and nontrivial fixed points [@abdesselam-2007], described in the article on that . The hierarchical recursion is the one-dimensional iteration which Abdesselam's construction perturbs, so the potential formulation of this article is where the two meet. The quartic coupling is relevant exactly when the kernel exponent is above half the dimension, which is the hierarchical form of the upper critical dimension: for $\alpha<d/2$ the interaction is long enough that the Gaussian fixed point governs, and for $\alpha>d/2$ the nontrivial fixed point does. The values $\alpha=d/2$ and, for short-range models, $d=4$, are the same statement in the parametrisation of Fisher, Ma and Nickel [@fisher-ma-nickel-1972], and in this model the relevance of the quartic coupling is the second diagonal entry of the linearisation at the Gaussian fixed point, computed in the spectrum article . Definitions and setting # Let $V$ be even, bounded below, with $\int e^{-V(s)}ds 0$. The hierarchical model with prior $e^{-V(s)}ds$ has the decimation recursion of the decimation article , and its block-spin law has a density because the tilt and the convolution of a density are densities. For $b\geq0$ the effective potential $\mathcal V_bV$ is defined by $$e^{-(\mathcal V_bV)(s)}=\frac{1}{Z_b(V)}\int_{\mathbb R^{m-1}}\exp\Bigl(b\sum_{a<a'}s_as_{a'}\Bigr)\prod_{a=1}^{m-1}e^{-V(s_a)}\,ds_1\cdots ds_{m-1},$$ with $s_m=s-\sum_{a<m}s_a$, and the scaled potential at exponent $\theta$ is $(\mathcal R_\theta V)(s)=(\mathcal V_bV)(L^{\theta}s)$ up to an additive constant. The potential formulation and the law formulation of the map article carry the same information: $e^{-(\mathcal V_bV)}$ is the density of $\mathcal T_b(e^{-V}ds)$. The constant in front is fixed by normalisation and plays no role in the flow of the shape of the potential; additive constants are the free energy increments of the free energy recursion and are dropped from the potential from here on. The Gaussian truncation # The one family the recursion preserves is the quadratic one, and on it the recursion is explicit. Let $V(s)=\tfrac{\mu}{2}s^2$ with $\mu>0$ and $b<1/(v(m-1))$, where $v=1/\mu$. Then $\mathcal V_bV$ is quadratic, with curvature $\mu'$ given by $$\frac{1}{\mu'}=\frac{m}{\mu-b(m-1)},$$ that is $\mu'=(\mu-b(m-1))/m$: the curvature flows affinely, and the variance recursion $v'=mv/(1-bv(m-1))$ is the same statement for $v=1/\mu$. A quartic potential is not mapped to a quartic potential: at $\tfrac{\mu}{2}s^2+\lambda s^4$ with $\lambda\neq0$ the first and second orders in $\lambda$ are again quartics in $s$, but the third order is not, and a sixth power appears with a coefficient proportional to $\lambda^3$. title: Hierarchical and Euclidean renormalisation
subtitle: Why the recursion closes here, what fails on the lattice, and how the model is used anyway.
summary: The hierarchical recursion is exact because a block has no boundary: all pairs between two children carry one coupling, so the decimated state is a function of the child states alone. On the Euclidean lattice a block has a boundary of codimension one, the effective interaction after decimation depends on the geometry of the boundary and not on block sums, and the decimated measure need not be Gibbsian. The hierarchical model is nevertheless the reference for power counting, for the epsilon expansion and for the local analysis of the renormalisation map.
text: The decimation identity is an identity, and not an approximation, because of one geometric fact: any two vertices in different children of a hierarchical block are at the same distance, so every pair joining two children carries the same coupling and the interaction between them is a function of the two block sums. A block has no boundary in the sense that no pair of its vertices is closer to the outside than another, and its children are congruent copies of itself. The recursion therefore closes on the law of one number. On $\mathbb Z^d$ none of this holds. A cube of side $L^n$ has a boundary of codimension one: the fraction of pairs at distance of order $L^n$ that join two neighbouring blocks is small, the number of nearest-neighbour edges crossing the boundary is of order $L^{(d-1)n}$ rather than $L^{dn}$, and the interaction between two blocks depends on whether they share a face, an edge or a corner. After one decimation step the effective interaction between two block magnetisations is a sum over a boundary whose size depends on the pair, and after two steps the interaction acquires a dependence on the shape of the interface. There is no finite-dimensional family of interactions closed under the operation, and there is a stronger obstruction: the decimated measure of a Gibbs measure need not be Gibbsian at all [@van-enter-fernandez-sokal-1993]. What the hierarchical model supplies in spite of this is the local structure of the renormalisation map itself: its fixed points, the dimension of the unstable manifold, the eigenvalue problem, the $\varepsilon$-expansion about the upper critical exponent, and the mechanism by which the nonlinearity is irrelevant [@gawedzki-kupiainen-1983]. Those are the inputs of the Euclidean renormalisation group, and the hierarchical model is the setting in which they can be established; the transfer is the programme of Gawedzki and Kupiainen for lattice field theory [@gawedzki-kupiainen-1980], and of the renormalisation-group analysis of critical $(\Phi^4)_3$ and related models [@brydges-mitter-scoppola-2003] [@bauerschmidt-brydges-slade-2019]. Definitions and setting # Let $L\geq2$. On the hierarchical lattice the level-$n$ block is the subgroup $\Lambda_n$ of the lattice article , its children are the cosets of $\Lambda_{n-1}$, and the decimation state at level $n$ is the law of the block spin $S_{\Lambda_n}$. On $\mathbb Z^d$ the level-$n$ block at $x$ is the cube $x+[0,L^n)^d\cap\mathbb Z^d$, its children are the $L^d$ subcubes of side $L^{n-1}$, and the decimation state at level $n$ is the joint law of the $L^d$ block magnetisations of the children together with the fine configuration inside them. An interaction is a function $\Phi$ on configurations; a decimation step maps the Gibbs measure with interaction $\Phi$ on the fine lattice to the law of the coarse variables. A family of interactions is closed if the decimated measure is again a Gibbs measure with an interaction in the family, for every member of the family and every choice of the coarse-graining scale. What closes the recursion # Suppose that a block $B$ is the disjoint union of $m$ children $B_1,\ldots,B_m$ and that the interaction is a sum over unordered pairs of a coupling that is constant on the set of pairs joining two given children. Then the energy of a configuration on $B$ is a function of the child configurations through the $m$ block sums alone, and the law of the $m$-tuple of block sums under the Gibbs measure of $B$ is determined by the interaction inside a child and by the $m(m-1)/2$ couplings between children. If in addition every child is isomorphic to $B$ with the same internal interaction, one decimation step is the map $\mathcal T_b$ of the map article , and the family of interactions on the scale of a block is closed. title: The block structure
subtitle: part 1
summary: Nested blocks, congruent children, and the decimation identity they make exact.
text: Three articles establish the object everything else rests on: a group whose balls are cosets of nested finite-index subgroups, with the same number of children at every scale. The child decomposition says that every pair of vertices in different children of a block sits at the top level of that block, which is what makes the energy split into the children plus one interaction between their sums. The decimation identity is that statement written as an identity for partition functions, and it is the whole reason the renormalisation group is exact here. The third article isolates what the argument actually uses, and carries it to the p-adic integers.

title: The renormalisation group
subtitle: part 2
summary: The map on block-spin laws, its fixed points, and the exponents read off them.
text: Decimation, rescaled, is one operator on laws on the line, and the model is an orbit of it. This part builds the operator, solves it exactly in the Gaussian case, and extracts from it the two numbers that matter: the multiplier of the linearised map, which gives the correlation-length exponent, and the growth of the block spin, which the autonomy of the recursion fixes for every fixed point of this model. From those two numbers the exponent dictionary follows by algebra. The remaining articles supply what the dictionary cannot: the non-Gaussian fixed point, the corrections to the power laws, and the two rigorous analyses of the fixed point that do not go through a small parameter.

title: Percolation, vectors, and the Euclidean comparison
subtitle: part 3
summary: What changes when the order parameter is a set, a vector, or a field on Z^d.
text: The same block structure carries models that are not the scalar spin model, and each one changes something specific. Percolation replaces the block-spin law by a cluster partition, and the mechanism that survives is amplification: two large clusters in sibling blocks are joined at a rate proportional to the product of their sizes. Vector spins make the block spin a vector, so the direction becomes an observable, and at criticality it does not settle. The phi-fourth truncation is where the infinite-dimensionality of the flow shows up, and the Euclidean comparison is where the exactness is lost.

title: Koch and Wittwer: the large-field problem
subtitle: reading map
text: This is the reading map for the three papers in which Hans Koch and Peter Wittwer proved that the hierarchical renormalisation map has a nontrivial fixed point with unbounded spins. The group is small and unusually homogeneous: the same two authors, one object, four papers, and a method that is the reason the papers are cited. The method is not a numerical certification. It is an analytic treatment of the large-field region , the part of the integral defining the effective potential in which the spin is too large for the perturbative expansion to converge and which, for an unbounded single-spin distribution, carries a non-negligible part of the measure. title: Hierarchical interaction and its level decomposition

The block at $x$ of level $n$ is the coset $x+G_n$; the children of a block $x+G_n$ are its cosets of $G_{n+1}$. Vertices at level $n$ are those in $G_n\setminus G_{n-1}$, and the shell at level $n$ is $G_n\setminus G_{n-1}$. Two examples carry the subject. The quadratic form of the tilt is $\sum_{a<a'}s_as_{a'}=\tfrac12\bigl(\bigl(\sum_as_a\bigr)^2-\sum_as_a^2\bigr)$, so the tilt rewards configurations whose sum is large in absolute value. title: Dilation covariance of the decimation operator
subtitle: proposition P4YS
text: For $\lambda>0$, with $\lambda_*\mu$ the law of $\lambda s$ under $\mu$, $$\mathcal T_b(\lambda_*\mu)=\lambda_*\bigl(\mathcal T_{b\lambda^2}\mu\bigr),\qquad \mathcal R_{\theta,b}(\lambda_*\mu)=\lambda_*\bigl(\mathcal R_{\theta,b\lambda^2}\mu\bigr).$$ Proof of dilation covariance Sampling $s_a$ from $\lambda_*\mu$ is the same as writing $s_a=\lambda t_a$ with $t_a$ sampled independently from $\mu$. The exponent becomes $b\lambda^2\sum_{a<a'}t_at_{a'}$, the normaliser becomes $Z_{b\lambda^2}(\mu)$, and the sum becomes $\lambda\sum_at_a$. Hence the law of $\sum_as_a$ is the image under multiplication by $\lambda$ of the law of $\sum_at_a$ computed with coupling $b\lambda^2$, which is the first identity. Multiplying by $L^{-\theta}$ afterwards gives the second, since dilations commute. The identity is the reason no separate analysis is needed at each scale: a factor $\lambda$ in the spin is a factor $\lambda^2$ in the coupling, so the pair $(\text{scale},\text{coupling})$ flows on a cone.

title: Continuity of decimation on compactly supported laws
subtitle: proposition E7NM
text: Fix $K<\infty$ and $B<\infty$. The map $(\mu,b)\mapsto\mathcal T_b\mu$ is continuous on the set of laws supported in $[-K,K]$ and couplings $b\in[0,B]$, for the topology of weak convergence, and $\mathcal T_b$ maps that set into the laws supported in $[-mK,mK]$. The normalisers are bounded below by $e^{-Bm(m-1)K^2/2}$, which is positive, so the normalised measures converge weakly by the same bounded convergence applied to $\mathbf 1_{A'}(\sum_as_a)$ tested against bounded continuous functions of $\sum_as_a$. The support statement is immediate from $\lvert s_a\rvert\leq K$. For the reverse inequality take $\phi=\mathbf 1_{\Lambda_n}/\sqrt{\lvert\Lambda_n\rvert}$, which has norm one: then $\langle\phi,A\phi\rangle=\sum_zJ(z)\lvert\Lambda_n\cap(\Lambda_n-z)\rvert/\lvert\Lambda_n\rvert$. For fixed $z$ the ratio tends to $1$ as $n\to\infty$, and it is at most $1$, so dominated convergence gives convergence to $\sum_zJ(z)$. text: Let $u_n=b_nv_n$ with $b_n=\beta J_n$. Then $u_n=g(u_{n-1})$, where $$g(u)=\frac{mu}{\lambda-(m-1)u},\qquad \lambda=L^{d+\alpha},$$ on the domain $u<\lambda/(m-1)$. The map $g$ has the fixed point $u^*=\dfrac{m(L^{\alpha}-1)}{m-1}$, and $g'(u^*)=\lambda/m=L^{\alpha}$. The critical orbit is $u_n\equiv u^*$; for $\beta<\beta_c$ one has $u_n\to0$ with ratio $L^{-\alpha}$, and for $\beta>\beta_c$ the orbit leaves the domain. title: Monomial directions and the linearised map at the Gaussian fixed point
subtitle: definition G5KM
text: For $K\geq1$ let $\mathcal P_K$ be the space of even polynomials of degree at most $2K$, with the basis $e_k(s)=s^{2k}$, $1\leq k\leq K$. The linearised map at $V^*$ is the derivative of $\Phi_{\theta_0}$ at $V^*$ in the direction of $\mathcal P_K$, that is the matrix $\Lambda$ with $$\Lambda_{jk}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\epsilon}\Big|_{\epsilon=0}\bigl[\Phi_{\theta_0}(V^*+\epsilon e_k)\bigr]_j,$$ where the subscript $j$ denotes the coefficient of $e_j$. The eigenvalue of the direction $e_k$ is the diagonal entry $\Lambda_{kk}$. The map is well defined on $\mathcal P_K$ because the integral is finite for a polynomial potential of even degree with a positive leading term, and the derivative exists because the dependence on $\epsilon$ is analytic in a neighbourhood of $0$. ## Statement {#section-statement}

The direction of degree $2k$ is relevant for the Gaussian fixed point exactly when $$k<\frac{d}{d-\alpha},$$ marginal when $k=d/(d-\alpha)$, and irrelevant otherwise. subtitle: proposition C4ND
text: For the spin model of the decimation article with $S_n=\sum_{x\in\Lambda_n}\sigma_x$ and free boundary conditions on $\Lambda_n$, $$\mathbb E_\beta[S_n^2]=L^{dn}\chi_n(\beta)$$ for every $\beta$ and every $n$. Proof of the block identity Expanding the square and taking expectations gives $\mathbb E[S_n^2]=\sum_{x,y\in\Lambda_n}\tau_n(x,y)$. Translation by any $x\in\Lambda_n$ preserves $\Lambda_n$ because $\Lambda_n$ is a subgroup, and preserves the finite-volume Gibbs measure because the Hamiltonian depends only on differences and the prior is a product; hence $\tau_n(x,y)=\tau_n(0,y-x)$. Since $\Lambda_n$ is a subgroup, $y-x\in\Lambda_n$ for $x,y\in\Lambda_n$, and summing over $x$ first gives $$\mathbb E[S_n^2]=\sum_{y\in\Lambda_n}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_n}\tau_n(0,y-x)=\lvert\Lambda_n\rvert\sum_{z\in\Lambda_n}\tau_n(0,z)=L^{dn}\chi_n(\beta),$$ the inner sum being independent of $y$ by the substitution $z=y-x$. The identity is the bridge between the two descriptions. The left side is what the decimation map controls directly, since the block-spin law is the state of the recursion; the right side is a correlation sum. The equality says the two growth rates are the same number: a block spin of typical size $L^{(d+\kappa)n/2}$ is exactly a block susceptibility growing like $L^{\kappa n}$. title: Critical coupling of the rescaled recursion
subtitle: definition B2SR
text: The critical coupling $b_c=b_c(m,\lambda)$ is the value of $b$ at which the orbit of the Ising initial law $\nu_0=\tfrac12(\delta_{-1}+\delta_1)$ under $\mathcal R_{\theta_0,b}$ neither converges to the point mass at $0$ nor leaves every compact set of laws with bounded variance; it is the value $b_c=\beta_cJ_1$ at which $\beta_c$ is the critical intensity of the model. The Gaussian laws form an invariant family, and the fixed points of the rescaled map inside that family are computed by one line of algebra. The computation is the reference point for everything else, so it is stated first.

title: Gaussian fixed points of the rescaled map
subtitle: proposition S8FR
text: Let $b>0$ and $\theta=\tfrac12(d+\alpha)$. The map $\mathcal R_{\theta,b}$ sends $N(0,v)$ to $N(0,w)$ with $$w=\frac{mv}{\lambda\bigl(1-bv(m-1)\bigr)},\qquad \lambda=L^{d+\alpha},$$ and has the unique Gaussian fixed point $N(0,v_b)$ with $v_b=\dfrac{\lambda-m}{\lambda b(m-1)}$. At $b=b_1^{(0)}=\dfrac{\lambda-m}{\lambda(m-1)}$ this fixed point is $N(0,1)$ and the multiplier of $\mathcal R_{\theta,b}$ in the variance direction is $\lambda/m=L^{\alpha}$. Proof of the fixed-point equation and the multiplier The first display is the variance recursion composed with the rescaling $v\mapsto L^{-2\theta}v$. A fixed point satisfies $v=\frac{mv}{\lambda(1-bv(m-1))}$ with $v>0$, which is $\lambda(1-bv(m-1))=m$, that is $v=v_b$; the normalisability condition $bv(m-1)<1$ holds because $bv_b(m-1)=1-m/\lambda<1$. At $b=b_1^{(0)}$ the variance is $v=\frac{\lambda-m}{\lambda(m-1)}\cdot\frac{\lambda(m-1)}{\lambda-m}=1$. The derivative of $w$ in $v$ at the fixed point is $\frac{m}{\lambda}\cdot\frac{1}{(1-bv(m-1))^2}=\frac{m}{\lambda}\cdot\frac{\lambda^2}{m^2}=\frac{\lambda}{m}$, using $1-bv_b(m-1)=m/\lambda$. For the Ising prior the fixed point is not Gaussian. This is the content of the theorem below; the proposition above shows only that the Gaussian candidate at the Ising critical coupling would have to be $N(0,v_{b_c})$, a single number, and the theorem says that the critical law is a different one. ## Statement {#section-statement}

title: Classical region and the crossover at alpha equal to half the dimension
subtitle: theorem D3LT
text: For $0<\alpha<d/2$ the critical orbit of the Ising initial law converges, after rescaling, to a Gaussian law, and the exponents take the classical values of the Gaussian fixed point . At $\alpha=d/2$ the nontrivial fixed point merges with the Gaussian one, $\lambda_1\to L^{d/2}$, and the classical values hold with logarithmic corrections. The arithmetic that connects the two statements is the proposition above: at $\alpha=d/2$ the classical correlation-length exponent is $1/\alpha=2/d$, so $\lambda_1=L^{d/2}$, and the two fixed points coincide at that value of the multiplier. The identification of the critical fixed point for $\alpha<d/2$ with the Gaussian one, and of the exponents with the classical values, is the content of the classical region in Bleher and Sinai [@bleher-sinai-1975]; the Euclidean counterpart at the same threshold is due to Aizenman and Fernandez [@aizenman-fernandez-1988]. The two theorems together describe a bifurcation: at $\alpha=d/2$ a nontrivial fixed point separates from the Gaussian one as $\alpha$ increases, taking over the critical behaviour. The exponents move continuously from the classical values at the threshold, which is why the classical formulas remain a good approximation just above $d/2$ and why the $\varepsilon$-expansion is organised in powers of $\alpha-d/2$ rather than in powers of a coupling. ## Examples and non-examples {#section-examples} The Gaussian case as the threshold member. title: The scalar fixed-point problem with unbounded spins
subtitle: definition C7QF
text: A fixed point is a potential $V^*$ with $\mathcal V_bV^*=V^*$ up to an additive constant, and the problem is to find one that is not quadratic. The quadratic fixed point exists for exactly one curvature at each coupling, is computed in the Gaussian article , and is the fixed point that loses stability at the marginal exponent; the non-quadratic fixed point is the one that takes over. Because the single-spin distribution has unbounded support, the domain of the map is not a space of bounded functions: the tilt and the constraint allow configurations in which one child carries an arbitrarily large spin, and the integral defining $\mathcal V_bV$ is finite only because the prior decays. The large-field region is the part of the domain of integration in which some $\lvert s_a\rvert$ exceeds a scale at which the perturbative expansion is valid, and controlling it is a precondition for the map to be defined at all as an operation on a space of potentials. ## Statement {#section-statement}

The same construction applies to the Dyson-Baker hierarchy, where the block structure comes from an expanding map rather than from the ultrametric blocks of the lattice article [@koch-wittwer-1994]. The eigenvalue statement that makes the fixed point a critical theory, with a one-dimensional unstable direction and the correlation-length exponent $\log L/\log\lambda_1$, is the one supplied by the general theory of the fixed-point article and by the analysis of the transformation in the companion paper [@koch-wittwer-1991]; it is not what the 1986 paper sets out to prove, and the wiki separates the two. ## Idea of the proof {#section-idea} The argument has three parts, and the first is the one that distinguishes it from everything else in this wiki. title: Trajectory between two fixed points
subtitle: definition D8WK
text: A trajectory between two fixed points is a sequence $(V_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$ of effective potentials, each in the domain of the map, such that $V_{j+1}$ is the image of $V_j$ for every $j$, and such that $V_j$ converges to the Gaussian fixed point as $j\to-\infty$ and to the nontrivial fixed point as $j\to+\infty$. The first limit is the ultraviolet, the second the infrared; the intermediate potentials describe the crossover, which is the region in which neither fixed point's linearisation controls the flow. For the hierarchical model the corresponding object is a sequence of laws $\nu_j=\mathcal R_{\theta_0,b}^{\,j}\nu_0$ under the single map of the autonomous form , and a trajectory between fixed points is an orbit whose two ends are the Gaussian and nontrivial fixed points of that map. In that case the trajectory is a property of a one-dimensional iteration and can be analysed by the methods of the fixed-point article . ## Statement {#section-statement}

title: Existence of a complete trajectory in three dimensions
subtitle: theorem D4XR
text: Let the field be three-dimensional with a modified free propagator, and let the interaction be a $\varphi^4$ perturbation with a small coupling. Then there is a sequence of effective potentials $(V_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$ satisfying the renormalisation recursion exactly, asymptotic to the ultraviolet Gaussian fixed point as $j\to-\infty$ and to the nontrivial infrared fixed point as $j\to+\infty$. The construction is nonperturbative in the sense that no order-by-order expansion is resummed: it produces the trajectory as the solution of a fixed-point equation in a Banach space of sequences. The statement is Theorem 1 of Abdesselam [@abdesselam-2007], with the summary of the method and of the role of the modified propagator in the six-page account of the same construction [@abdesselam-2009]. The infrared endpoint is an analogue of the Wilson-Fisher fixed point: it is the nontrivial fixed point of the model with the modified propagator rather than a statement about the unmodified three-dimensional $\varphi^4$ theory, whose renormalisation-group trajectory is constructed by different means in the work of Brydges, Mitter and Scoppola [@brydges-mitter-scoppola-2003]. ## Idea of the proof {#section-idea} The three steps below are the ones the account of the construction names; the estimates are in the paper. text: Let $n\geq0$, let $B,B'$ be distinct children of $\Lambda_{n+1}$, let $x\in B$ and $y\in B'$, and let $I=\lvert K^{B}_x\rvert$ and $I'=\lvert K^{B'}_y\rvert$ computed with the bonds inside $B$ and $B'$ respectively. title: Dyson's conjecture for the vector model and the critical direction
subtitle: theorem B9HL
text: Let $r\geq2$, let the interaction be $U(x,y)=-l_nL^{-2n}\langle\sigma_x,\sigma_y\rangle$ at level $n$, and let the prior be uniform on $\mathbb S^{r-1}$. subtitle: proposition X5QM
text: Suppose that a block $B$ is the disjoint union of $m$ children $B_1,\ldots,B_m$ and that the interaction is a sum over unordered pairs of a coupling that is constant on the set of pairs joining two given children. title: The Euclidean block has a boundary and its decimation is not a function of block sums
subtitle: proposition Z7MR
text: Let $B=[0,L^n)^d\cap\mathbb Z^d$ with $n\geq1$ and $L\geq2$, and let $B_1,B_2$ be two subcubes of side $L^{n-1}$. The number of unordered pairs $\{x,y\}$ with $x\in B_1$, $y\in B_2$ is $L^{2d(n-1)}$, and the number of such pairs that are nearest neighbours is at most $dL^{d(n-1)}$. Moreover the fraction of nearest-neighbour edges of $\mathbb Z^d$ that join two distinct $L$-blocks equals $1/L$, independently of the scale. Proof of the boundary counts The two cubes each have $L^{d(n-1)}$ vertices, so there are $L^{2d(n-1)}$ unordered pairs. Each vertex has $2d$ neighbours, so the number of neighbouring pairs between the two cubes is at most $2dL^{d(n-1)}/2=dL^{d(n-1)}$: this is the bound for the count of pairs, and the exponent $d(n-1)$ against $2d(n-1)$ is the statement that only a fraction $L^{-d(n-1)}$ of the pairs are nearest neighbours. For the fraction of edges, count in the infinite lattice. Each block of the $L$-partition contains $L^d$ vertices; the nearest-neighbour edges with both endpoints in it are $dL^{d-1}(L-1)$, since there are $d$ directions and $L^{d-1}(L-1)$ edges in each. The number of edges per vertex of $\mathbb Z^d$ is $d$, so the number of edges per block is $dL^d$, and the fraction with both endpoints in the same block is $\frac{dL^{d-1}(L-1)}{dL^d}=\frac{L-1}{L}$. title: Block-spin transformations can destroy the Gibbs property
subtitle: theorem Q2LN
text: There are translation-invariant Gibbs measures for finite-range lattice interactions whose image under a block-spin transformation is not a Gibbs measure for any interaction, and there are models for which the image is Gibbsian but with an interaction that is not absolutely summable. Consequently position-space decimation does not define a map on a space of interactions in general [@van-enter-fernandez-sokal-1993]. The reason is a long-range dependence in the coarse variables that is invisible in the fine ones: conditioning on the outside of a region in the coarse lattice constrains the fine configuration in a way that is not mediated by finitely many coarse variables, so the conditional probabilities of the coarse measure fail the Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle form. The hierarchical model is immune because its coarse variables are the block sums and a block interacts with the rest of the lattice through its sum alone, so conditioning on the outside of a block constrains the block only through one number. ## Consequences and applications {#section-consequences} The reference model for the local analysis. The renormalisation map of a hierarchical model is a nonlinear map on a space of measures with exponential moments, and the analysis of its fixed points, its unstable manifold and the $\varepsilon$-expansion can be carried out completely, as in the Bleher–Sinai article .
